claim: Receptors signal by switching between resting (C) and active (O) shapes ('gating') under the influence of agonists.
source: Receptors signal by switching between resting (C) and active (O) shapes ('gating') under the influence of agonists.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about receptor function that draws from established scientific understanding of receptor biology.

claim: The receptor's maximum response depends on the difference in agonist binding energy, O minus C.
source: The receptor's maximum response depends on the difference in agonist binding energy, O minus C.
evidence: This statement is supported by the theoretical framework and experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly through the efficiency measurements.

claim: In nicotinic receptors, efficiency (η) represents the fraction of agonist binding energy applied to a local rearrangement (an induced fit) that initiates gating.
source: In nicotinic receptors, efficiency (η) represents the fraction of agonist binding energy applied to a local rearrangement (an induced fit) that initiates gating.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of the manuscript, supported by experimental measurements and theoretical analysis.

claim: In this receptor, free energy changes in gating and binding can be interchanged by the conversion factor η.
source: In this receptor, free energy changes in gating and binding can be interchanged by the conversion factor η.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the mathematical relationships (Equation 2) and experimental data showing the correlation between binding and gating energies.

claim: Efficiencies estimated from concentration-response curves (23 agonists, 53 mutations) sort into five discrete classes (%): 0.56 (17), 0.51(32), 0.45(13), 0.41(26), and 0.31(12).
source: Efficiencies estimated from concentration-response curves (23 agonists, 53 mutations) sort into five discrete classes (%): 0.56 (17), 0.51(32), 0.45(13), 0.41(26), and 0.31(12), implying that there are 5 C versus O binding site structural pairs.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental measurements from CRCs and x-means cluster analysis as shown in Figures 4 and 7.

claim: There are 5 C versus O binding site structural pairs.
source: Efficiencies estimated from concentration-response curves (23 agonists, 53 mutations) sort into five discrete classes (%): 0.56 (17), 0.51(32), 0.45(13), 0.41(26), and 0.31(12), implying that there are 5 C versus O binding site structural pairs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of five discrete efficiency classes, suggesting distinct structural configurations.

claim: Within each class efficacy and affinity are correlated linearly.
source: Within each class efficacy and affinity are corelated linearly, but multiple classes hide this relationship.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the efficiency plots in Figure 4B showing linear correlations within each efficiency class.

claim: Multiple classes hide the relationship between efficacy and affinity.
source: Within each class efficacy and affinity are corelated linearly, but multiple classes hide this relationship.
evidence: This is shown by the lack of global correlation when all agonists are considered together, but clear correlations within individual classes.

claim: η unites agonist binding with receptor gating.
source: η unites agonist binding with receptor gating and calibrates one link in a chain of coupled domain rearrangements that comprises the allosteric transition of the protein.
evidence: This is supported by the mathematical framework (Equation 2) and experimental data showing the relationship between binding and gating energies.

claim: η calibrates one link in a chain of coupled domain rearrangements that comprises the allosteric transition of the protein.
source: η unites agonist binding with receptor gating and calibrates one link in a chain of coupled domain rearrangements that comprises the allosteric transition of the protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the efficiency measurements and the proposed model of sequential domain rearrangements during receptor activation.

claim: Each agonist has two affinities that measure how strongly it binds to resting and active target sites.
source: Each agonist has two affinities that measure how strongly it binds to resting and active target sites, and an efficacy that measures how well it activates once bound (Cecchini and Changeux, 2022; Ehlert, 2015; Foreman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge in receptor pharmacology, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Efficacy measures how well an agonist activates once bound.
source: Each agonist has two affinities that measure how strongly it binds to resting and active target sites, and an efficacy that measures how well it activates once bound (Cecchini and Changeux, 2022; Ehlert, 2015; Foreman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge in receptor pharmacology, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Efficiency (η; eta) is the correlation between efficacy and affinity and is the receptor's output/input energy ratio.
source: A third agonist property, efficiency (η; eta), is the correlation between efficacy and affinity and is the receptor's output/input energy ratio (Nayak et al., 2019).
evidence: This definition is supported by citation to previous work and is the central concept of the manuscript.

claim: AChRs are five subunit, ligand-gated ion channels that have two neurotransmitter sites in the extracellular domain (ECD).
source: AChRs are five subunit, ligand-gated ion channels that have two neurotransmitter sites in the extracellular domain (ECD), and a narrow equatorial gate in the lumen of the transmembrane domain (TMD) that governs the passive flow of cations across the membrane (Gharpure et al., 2020; Unwin, 1995; Zarkadas et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about AChRs, supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: AChRs have a narrow equatorial gate in the lumen of the transmembrane domain (TMD) that governs the passive flow of cations across the membrane.
source: AChRs are five subunit, ligand-gated ion channels that have two neurotransmitter sites in the extracellular domain (ECD), and a narrow equatorial gate in the lumen of the transmembrane domain (TMD) that governs the passive flow of cations across the membrane (Gharpure et al., 2020; Unwin, 1995; Zarkadas et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about AChRs, supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: AChRs are allosteric proteins that alternate spontaneously between global off (C, closed-channel) and on (O, open-channel) conformations.
source: AChRs are allosteric proteins that alternate spontaneously between global off (C, closed-channel) and on (O, open-channel) conformations in which each neurotransmitter site binds agonists weakly (with low affinity; LA) or strongly (with high affinity; HA) (Cecchini and Changeux, 2022; Jackson, 2006; Phillips, 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about AChR function, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Each neurotransmitter site binds agonists weakly (with low affinity; LA) in the C conformation or strongly (with high affinity; HA) in the O conformation.
source: AChRs are allosteric proteins that alternate spontaneously between global off (C, closed-channel) and on (O, open-channel) conformations in which each neurotransmitter site binds agonists weakly (with low affinity; LA) or strongly (with high affinity; HA) (Cecchini and Changeux, 2022; Jackson, 2006; Phillips, 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about AChR binding properties, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The AChR neurotransmitter sites and gate are separated by ~60 Å.
source: The AChR neurotransmitter sites and gate are separated by ~60 Å, but both regions change structure and function within the gating isomerization, CLA⇄OHA.
evidence: This is a structural measurement based on known AChR structures.

claim: Both the neurotransmitter sites and gate regions change structure and function within the gating isomerization.
source: The AChR neurotransmitter sites and gate are separated by ~60 Å, but both regions change structure and function within the gating isomerization, CLA⇄OHA.
evidence: This is inferred from structural and functional studies of AChR activation.

claim: In adult-type AChRs without any bound agonists, the probability of the O conformation (PO) is small (~10–6) so baseline current is negligible.
source: In adult-type AChRs and without any bound agonists, the probability of the O conformation (PO) is small (~10–6) so baseline current is negligible (Jackson, 1986; Nayak et al., 2012; Purohit and Auerbach, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements cited from previous studies.

claim: When both agonist sites are occupied by the neurotransmitter ACh, the increase in favorable binding free energy realized in the spontaneous isomerization from C to O increases PO substantially (to ~0.96).
source: However, when both agonist sites are occupied by the neurotransmitter ACh, the increase in favorable binding free energy realized in the spontaneous isomerization from C to O increases PO substantially (to ~0.96), to generate a cellular current (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and represents a key functional property of AChRs.

claim: For ACh at adult-type binding sites KdC = 174 μM (ΔGLA = −5.1 kcal/mol) and KdO = 29 nM (ΔGHA = −10.2 kcal/mol).
source: For ACh at adult-type binding sites KdC = 174 μM (ΔGLA = −5.1 kcal/mol) and KdO = 29 nM (ΔGHA = −10.2 kcal/mol) (Jadey and Auerbach, 2012).
evidence: These are experimental measurements cited from previous work.

claim: In adult-type AChRs the 2 neurotransmitter binding sites are approximately equivalent and independent.
source: In adult-type AChRs the 2 neurotransmitter binding sites are approximately equivalent and independent and there is no significant input of external energy (Nayak and Auerbach, 2017), so
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: There is no significant input of external energy in adult-type AChR activation.
source: In adult-type AChRs the 2 neurotransmitter binding sites are approximately equivalent and independent and there is no significant input of external energy (Nayak and Auerbach, 2017), so
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: A small, thermalized ligand can deliver only a small force to a large receptor.
source: Unlike voltage and mechanical stimuli, a small, thermalized ligand can deliver only a small force to a large receptor (Howard, 2001).
evidence: This is a physical principle supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The tiny momentum imparted to the protein by the ligand is obscured by those from collisions with water molecules.
source: The tiny momentum imparted to the protein by the ligand is obscured by those from collisions with water molecules.
evidence: This is a physical principle based on thermodynamics and molecular dynamics.

claim: In the absence of external energy, agonists promote conformational change only by providing more favorable (stabilizing) binding energy to active compared to resting states that interconvert spontaneously.
source: In the absence of external energy, agonists promote conformational change only by providing more favorable (stabilizing) binding energy to active compared to resting states that interconvert spontaneously.
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of allosteric receptor activation supported by thermodynamic considerations.

claim: The mechanism of agonist-promoted conformational change likely pertains to all large receptors activated by small agonists.
source: This mechanism likely pertains to all large receptors activated by small agonists.
evidence: This is a speculative generalization based on physical principles.

claim: The agonist-dependent free energy changes in gating (ΔGHA-ΔGLA) and in binding (ΔGHA) are interchangeable, with η as the conversion factor.
source: Accordingly, the agonist-dependent free energy changes in gating (ΔGHA-ΔGLA) and in binding (ΔGHA) are interchangeable, with η as the conversion factor.
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical definition of efficiency (Equation 2).

claim: Efficacy (λ) is a free energy difference and the maximum amount the agonist can deliver to the receptor's gating machinery.
source: Again, efficacy (λ) is a free energy difference and the maximum amount the agonist can deliver to the receptor's gating machinery, and efficiency (η) is a free energy ratio and this amount normalized by the ligand's maximum binding energy.
evidence: This is a definition derived from the theoretical framework presented in the manuscript.

claim: Efficiency (η) is a free energy ratio and this amount normalized by the ligand's maximum binding energy.
source: Again, efficacy (λ) is a free energy difference and the maximum amount the agonist can deliver to the receptor's gating machinery, and efficiency (η) is a free energy ratio and this amount normalized by the ligand's maximum binding energy.
evidence: This is a definition derived from the theoretical framework presented in the manuscript.

claim: An η value can be calculated from the ratio of logarithms of the 2 dissociation constants for every agonist of every receptor.
source: We propse that an η value can be calculated from the ratio of logarithms of the 2 dissociation constants for every agonist of every receptor.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the universal nature of the two-affinity model for agonist binding.

claim: In AChRs η has a physiochemical meaning because KdC and KdO derive mainly from a pair of induced fit rearrangements at the ligand site.
source: In AChRs η does have a physiochemical meaning because KdC and KdO derive mainly from a pair of induced fit rearrangements at the ligand site.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and the proposed model of catch-and-hold rearrangements.

claim: Although bind and gate are usually denoted as single-step events, in AChRs both are composite reactions that harbor intermediate states that are too short-lived to be detected individually and directly.
source: Although bind and gate are usually denoted as single-step events (Figure 1B), in AChRs both are composite reactions that harbor intermediate states that are too short-lived to be detected individually and directly (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from kinetic analysis and supported by the model presented in Figure 2.

claim: Induced fits are common in biological systems.
source: Induced fits are common, and undetected intermediate states have been invoked with great success previosuly to explain experimental results (for example ES in enzymology, and AC in pharmacology).
evidence: This is established knowledge from enzymology and pharmacology.

claim: The main undetected intermediate states in AChR activation are AC (the encounter complex) and ACHA (a high affinity and closed channel state).
source: The main undetected intermediate states are AC, the encounter complex (inside bind) and ACHA, a high affinity and closed channel state (inside gate).
evidence: This is proposed based on the model shown in Figure 2 and kinetic analysis.

claim: The 2 agonist-dependent induced fit rearrangements are called catch (AC⇄ACLA) and hold (ACLA⇄ACHA).
source: Black, the 2 agonist-dependent induced fit rearrangements are called catch (AC⇄ACLA) and hold (ACLA⇄ACHA).
evidence: This is the nomenclature introduced in the manuscript for the two stages of the induced fit.

claim: Diffusion (A+C⇄AC) and receptor conformation changes in other domains (ACHA⇄AO) are approximately agonist-independent.
source: Gray, diffusion (A+C⇄AC) and receptor conformation changes in other domains (ACHA⇄AO) are approximately agonist-independent (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from experimental observations and kinetic analysis.

claim: An η class indicates that catch and hold are linked in a linear free energy relationship (LFER).
source: An η class indicates that catch and hold are linked in a linear free energy relationship (LFER; dashed lines) (Howard, 2001).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of discrete efficiency classes and supported by citation.

claim: For relative agonist actions, the energy change in catch determines KdC and the energy change in hold determines the coupling constant.
source: For relative agonist actions, the energy change in catch (brown) determines KdC and the energy change in hold (blue) determines the coupling constant.
evidence: This is inferred from the model and the relationship between energy changes and equilibrium constants.

claim: η is the fraction of the total binding energy applied to hold and 1-η is the fraction applied to catch.
source: η is the fraction of the total applied to hold (blue/black) and η is the fraction apllied to catch (brown/black).
evidence: This is derived from the definition of efficiency and the energy landscape model.

claim: Agonist affinity and efficacy differ substantially, but η is constant within a class and depends only on the left-right position of ACLA in the reaction.
source: Agonist affinity and efficacy differ substantially, but η is constant and depends only on the left-right position of ACLA in the reaction.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of constant η within classes despite varying affinities and efficacies.

claim: For BzTMA, EC50 = 1070 μM, POmax = 0.60, KdC = 930 μM, KdO = 650 nM, and η = 0.51.
evidence: These are experimental measurements reported in Table 1.

claim: For Dec, EC50 = 190 μM, POmax = 0.79, KdC = 90 μM, KdO = 140 nM, and η = 0.41.
evidence: These are experimental measurements reported in Table 1.

claim: For SCh, EC50 = 20 μM, POmax = 0.84, KdC = 50 μM, KdO = 20 nM, and η = 0.45.
evidence: These are experimental measurements reported in Table 1.

claim: For BzTEA, EC50 = 2 μM, POmax = 0.85, KdC = 0.80 μM, KdO = 3 nM, and η = 0.29.
evidence: These are experimental measurements reported in Table 1.

claim: For TriMA, EC50 = 16000 μM, POmax = 0.78, KdC = 7720 μM, KdO = 12580 nM, and η = 0.57.
evidence: These are experimental measurements reported in Table 1.

claim: SCh is 10% more efficient than Dec.
source: SCh is 10% more efficient than Dec, which is the root cause of the abovementioned mismatch between POmax and potency.
evidence: This is calculated from the measured efficiency values (0.45 vs 0.41) reported in Table 1.

claim: Given L0, agonist efficiency can be calculated from a single CRC.
source: Figure 3 shows that given L0, agonist efficiency can be calculated from a single CRC.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental approach shown in Figure 3.

claim: Error arising from errors in POmax and EC50 are small because η is the ratio of two logarithms.
source: Because η is the ratio of two logarithms, error arising from errors in POmax and EC50 are small (Indurthi and Auerbach, 2021).
evidence: This is a mathematical property supported by citation to previous work.

claim: X-means cluster analysis of all 23 agonist η values indicates that there are 5 groups with means: 0.32±0.035, 0.41±0.005, 0.45±0.014, 0.51±.008 and 0.55±0.015.
source: An x-means cluster analysis of all 23 agonist η values indicates that there are 5 groups (mean ± sd): 0.32±0.035, 0.41±0.005, 0.45±0.014, 0.51±.008 and 0.55±0.015.
evidence: This is the result of statistical cluster analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The neurotransmitter ACh, its breakdown product choline (Cho), and the partial agonists carbamylcholine (CCh) and nicotine all belong to the η~0.51 class.
source: The neurotransmitter ACh, its breakdown product choline (Cho), and the partial agonists carbamylcholine (CCh) and nicotine all belong to the η~0.51 class.
evidence: This is based on the efficiency measurements and cluster analysis shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The η~0.41 class includes ligands that have a bridge nitrogen (for instance, Ebt) as well as others that do not (for instance, Dec and TMP).
source: The second-most common class, η~0.41, includes ligands that have a bridge nitrogen (for instance, Ebt) as well as others that do not (for instance, Dec and TMP).
evidence: This is based on the efficiency measurements and structural analysis shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Small ligands (for instance, TriMA, MW 60) appear to be the most efficient.
source: Small ligands (for instance, TriMA, MW 60) appear to be the most efficient and large rigid ligands (for instance, varenicline, MW 211) appear to be the least efficient.
evidence: This is an observation based on the efficiency measurements and molecular weights of the agonists.

claim: Large rigid ligands (for instance, varenicline, MW 211) appear to be the least efficient.
source: Small ligands (for instance, TriMA, MW 60) appear to be the most efficient and large rigid ligands (for instance, varenicline, MW 211) appear to be the least efficient.
evidence: This is an observation based on the efficiency measurements and molecular weights of the agonists.

claim: η values estimated from the slopes for the 23 agonists are: 0.31±0.018, 0.41±0.002, 0.46±0.004, 0.51±0.002 and 0.56±0.008.
source: η values estimated from the slopes for the 23 agonists (Figure 4B) are the same as from the x-mean cluster analysis (Figure 4A) (mean ± sd): 0.31±0.018, 0.41±0.002, 0.46±0.004, 0.51±0.002 and 0.56±0.008.
evidence: These are calculated from the efficiency plots shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Affinity and efficacy are correlated significantly within the 3 classes having >2 members (Pearson's correlation test p-values for η=0.41 and 0.51,<0.0001, and for η=0.56, 0.019).
source: Affinity and efficacy are correlated significantly within the 3 classes having >2 members (19 agonists; Pearson's correlation test p-values for η=0.41 and 0.51,<0.0001, and for η=0.56, 0.019).
evidence: This is the result of statistical analysis of the efficiency plot data.

claim: The slopes for the 3 classes with >2 members are significantly different (ANCOVA, F=129, p<0.001).
source: Also, the slopes for these 3 classes are significantly different (ANCOVA, F=129, p<0.001).
evidence: This is the result of statistical analysis comparing the slopes of the efficiency plots.

claim: In AChRs, agonists having the same affinity can have different efficacies, and vice versa.
source: Figure 4B shows that in AChRs, agonists having the same affinity can have different efficacies, and vice versa.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the efficiency plot in Figure 4B showing multiple classes with different slopes.

claim: Absent classification of an agonist according to η there is no global correlation between efficacy and affinity.
source: Absent classification of an agonist according to η (imagine all symbols the same color) there is no global correlation between these two agonist properties.
evidence: This is inferred from the efficiency plot showing that correlations only appear within individual classes.

claim: A linear correlation between log affinity and log efficacy is clear within each class.
source: However, a linear correlation between log affinity and log efficacy is clear within each class.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the efficiency plots in Figure 4B.

claim: In AChRs, the presence of multiple η classes precludes a global correlation between efficacy and affinity.
source: In AChRs, the presence of multiple η classes precludes a global correlation between efficacy and affinity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that correlations exist within but not across efficiency classes.

claim: The substitution αD200A reduces the efficiency of 4 of the 5 agonists to 0.33±0.04.
source: The substitution αD200A reduces the efficiency of 4 of the 5 agonists to 0.33±0.04 (mean ± sd), or to about the same level as with αY190A with ACh.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements reported in Table 2.

claim: The exceptional ligand for αD200A was TMA for which η remained relatively high at 0.48.
source: The exceptional ligand was TMA for which η remained relatively high at 0.48.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements reported in Table 2.

claim: In αK145A, η for all 5 agonists was 0.41±0.03.
source: In contrast, in αK145A η for all 5 agonists was 0.41±0.03.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements reported in Table 2.

claim: The mutation αK145A reduces η for ACh, CCh and TMA but not significantly for Ebx and Ebt.
source: Interestingly, this mutation reduces η for ACh, CCh and TMA but not significantly for Ebx and Ebt.
evidence: This is based on comparison of efficiency values in Table 2 with wild-type values.

claim: The mutation αW149A increases η for ACh to 0.60.
source: Note that the mutation αW149A increases η for ACh to 0.60 (Purohit et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Mutations at αG153 reduce η for Cho, DMP, TMA and nicotine to 0.41±0.03 on average, or by ~25%.
source: After converting the published equilibrium constants to ΔGLA and ΔGHA, the results indicate that on average the mutations reduce η for Cho, DMP, TMA and nicotine to 0.41±0.03 (mean ± sd), or by ~25%.
evidence: This is based on reanalysis of data from a cited previous study (Jadey et al., 2013).

claim: αG153S reduces η of Ebt from 0.42 to 0.31, or by ~25%.
source: To these we add the new result that αG153S reduces η of Ebt from 0.42 to 0.31, or also by ~25%.
evidence: This is based on new experimental measurements reported in Table 2.

claim: Mutant η values segregate into the same 5 η classes as agonists: 0.33±0.03, 0.40±0.02, 0.44±0.01, 0.49±0.01 and 0.56±0.03.
source: Mutant η values (mean ± sd) segregate into the same 5 η classes that were apparent with agonists: 0.33±0.03, 0.40±0.02, 0.44±0.01, 0.49±0.01 and 0.56±0.03.
evidence: This is based on x-means cluster analysis of mutation data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The η classes that were under-represented and poorly defined with agonists are more common and clearer with mutations.
source: The η classes that were under-represented and poorly defined with agonists (Figure 4B) are more common and clearer with mutations.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the cluster analyses in Figures 4 and 7.

claim: The distribution of η values from mutations (1-slope) is: 0.32±0.007, 0.40±0.004, 0.44±0.003, 0.49±0.002 and 0.56±0.007.
source: The distribution of η values (1-slope) is (mean ± sd): 0.32±0.007, 0.40±0.004, 0.44±0.003, 0.49±0.002 and 0.56±0.007, with all slopes being significantly different (ANCOVA, F-value, 63.35; p-value,<0.0001).
evidence: This is calculated from the slopes of the plots in Figure 7B.

claim: All slopes in the mutation efficiency plot are significantly different (ANCOVA, F-value, 63.35; p-value,<0.0001).
source: The distribution of η values (1-slope) is (mean ± sd): 0.32±0.007, 0.40±0.004, 0.44±0.003, 0.49±0.002 and 0.56±0.007, with all slopes being significantly different (ANCOVA, F-value, 63.35; p-value,<0.0001).
evidence: This is the result of statistical analysis of the mutation efficiency plots.

claim: Combining the results for agonists and mutations, the overall distribution of η (relative prevalence) is: 0.56 (17%), 0.51 (31%), 0.45 (13%), 0.41 (26%), and 0.31 (12%).
source: Combining the results for agonists and mutations, the overall distribution of η (relative prevalence) is: 0.56 (17%), 0.51 (31%), 0.45 (13%), 0.41 (26%), and 0.31 (12%).
evidence: This is calculated from the combined dataset of agonists and mutations.

claim: The 0.51 (example, ACh) and 0.41 (example, Ebt) classes predominate.
source: As was the case with agonists and mutations separately, the 0.51 (example, ACh) and 0.41 (example, Ebt) classes predominate.
evidence: This is based on the prevalence data showing these two classes account for 57% of all measurements.

claim: Efficiency is the missing link that connects binding to gating.
source: Efficiency is the missing link that connects binding to gating (Equation 2).
evidence: This is the central conclusion of the manuscript, supported by the mathematical framework and experimental data.

claim: In AChRs, KdC and KdO are set mainly by energy changes in a pair of local rearrangements of the binding site (the catch-and-hold induced fit).
source: In AChRs, KdC and KdO are set mainly by energy changes in a pair of local rearrangements of the binding site (the catch-and-hold induced fit), with η being the fraction of the total used to initiate the allosteric transition of the receptor.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism based on the efficiency measurements and kinetic analysis.

claim: η calibrates the fundamental connection that defines receptor action.
source: As such, η calibrates the fundamental connection that defines receptor action.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the role of efficiency in linking binding and gating.

claim: Converting ligand binding energy into energy for an otherwise unfavorable protein conformational change is an induced fit.
source: Converting ligand binding energy into energy for an otherwise unfavorable protein conformational change is an induced fit.
evidence: This is a definition based on established concepts in protein biochemistry.

claim: Without an agonist present, both catch and hold rearrangements (of an aromatic pocket) are energetically unfavorable and generate the high barrier to unliganded opening.
source: We assume that without an agonist present, both catch and hold rearrangements (of an aromatic pocket) are energetically unfavorable and generate the high barrier to unliganded opening (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an assumption based on the low probability of unliganded opening and the energy landscape model.

claim: In enzymes, a fraction of substrate binding energy is used to promote a local protein rearrangement that stabilizes the reaction transition state.
source: In enzymes, a fraction of substrate binding energy is used to promote a local protein rearrangement that stabilizes the reaction transition state (Richard, 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge from enzymology, supported by citation.

claim: In AChRs, neurotransmitter binding energy is divided equally between two stages of an intrinsically unfavorable rearrangement that forms the LA and HA complexes and starts the gating isomerization.
source: In AChRs, neurotransmitter binding energy is divided equally between two stages of an intrinsically unfavorable rearrangement that forms the LA and HA complexes and starts the gating isomerization.
evidence: This is inferred from the efficiency measurements showing approximately equal division of energy between catch and hold for the predominant classes.

claim: η quantifies the split in ligand binding energy between the two steps in the catch-and-hold induced fit.
source: In brief, η quantifies the split in ligand binding energy between the two steps in the catch-and-hold induced fit (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is the interpretation of efficiency based on the energy landscape model.

claim: Agonists having radically different resting affinities and efficacies can have the same η.
source: Agonists having radically different resting affinities and efficacies can have the same η.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data showing ACh and choline have the same efficiency despite very different affinities and efficacies.

claim: ACh (KdC = 175 μM, POmax = 0.96) and choline (KdC = 4 mM, POmax = 0.05) both divide their binding energy equally between catch and hold.
source: For example, ACh (KdC = 175 μM, POmax = 0.96) and choline (KdC = 4 mM, POmax = 0.05) both divide their binding energy equally between catch and hold.
evidence: This is based on the efficiency measurements showing both agonists belong to the η~0.51 class.

claim: In AChRs, agonists segregate into discrete η classes within which all members use approximately the same fraction of their post-diffusion binding energy for catch.
source: In AChRs, agonists segregate into discrete ηclasses within which all members use approximately the same fraction of their post-diffusion binding energy for catch.
evidence: This is based on the cluster analysis showing five discrete efficiency classes.

claim: Five η classes have been identified with catch percentages ranging from 47% to 71%.
source: So far we have identified 5 η classes with catch percentages ranging from 47% to 71% (Table 1).
evidence: This is calculated from the efficiency values in Table 1 (1-η gives the catch percentage).

claim: Larger ligands may apply a larger percentage of their binding energy to catch.
source: Below, we discuss the possibility that larger ligands apply a larger percentage of their binding energy to catch.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that small ligands appear more efficient.

claim: The existence of an η class indicates that in AChRs the two binding energy (structure) changes in bind and gate are correlated and joined in a linear free energy relationship (LFER).
source: η classes are notable because its two component energy changes (Equation 3) are realized in bind and in gate, usually considered to be qualitatively different processes (Figure 1B). Nevertheless, the existence of an η class indicates that in AChRs these two binding energy (structure) changes are correlated and joined in a linear free energy relationship (LFER) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of discrete efficiency classes with linear correlations within each class.

claim: Any change in bind (catch) free energy compels one in gate (hold), reciprocally.
source: Any change in bind (catch) free energy compels one in gate (hold), reciprocally.
evidence: This is a consequence of the LFER relationship between catch and hold.

claim: Rather than being independent processes, bind and gate are completely entangled even if they are depicted as different dimensions of a reaction scheme.
source: Rather than being independent processes, bind and gate are completely entangled even if they are depicted as different dimensions of a reaction scheme (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the LFER relationship and the efficiency measurements.

claim: An empirical η value can be calculated for every agonist of every receptor.
source: Although an empirical η value can be calculated for every agonist of every receptor, the generality of η classes is less certain.
evidence: This follows from the universal nature of the two-affinity model for agonist binding.

claim: The generality of η classes is less certain than the ability to calculate η.
source: Although an empirical η value can be calculated for every agonist of every receptor, the generality of η classes is less certain.
evidence: This is a cautious statement acknowledging limited data from other receptor systems.

claim: Some results suggest that a catch-and-hold induced fit, with stages linked in a LFER, is not uncommon in other receptors.
source: The components, KdC and KdO for many agonists, have not been measured extensively in other receptors, but some results suggest that a catch-and-hold induced fit, with stages linked in a LFER, is not uncommon.
evidence: This is based on limited data from other receptor systems mentioned in the discussion.

claim: It is likely that an increase in affinity caused by a local binding site rearrangement inside the gating isomerization is typical.
source: Regarding hold, it is likely that an increase in affinity caused by a local binding site rearrangement inside the gating isomerization is typical (ACLA⇄ACHA).
evidence: This is based on observations in multiple receptor systems cited in the discussion.

claim: In enzymes and receptors, agonists induce a 'clamshell' closure of the ligand site that is associated with increased binding strength.
source: In enzymes and receptors, agonists induce a 'clamshell' closure of the ligand site that is associated with increased binding strength (Armstrong and Gouaux, 2000; Masiulis et al., 2019; Pless and Lynch, 2009; Traynelis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: In many receptors agonists increase the opening rate constant as well as PO.
source: Also, in many receptors agonists increase the opening rate constant as well as PO (Clements et al., 1998; Clements and Westbrook, 1991; Maconochie et al., 1994) indicating that the stabilization by the lgiadn of an otherwise unfavorable rearrangement (the affinity increase) occurs early in the isomerization (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to kinetic studies.

claim: In other receptors an ACHA intermediate state has been detected directly in single-channel currents.
source: Finally, in other receptors an ACHA intermediate state has been detected directly in single-channel currents (Lape et al., 2008; Shi et al., 2023) or identified in structures (Sauguet et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies in other receptor systems.

claim: The first step in the induced fit (catch) serves a purpose.
source: Regarding catch, this first step in the induced fit serves a purpose (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and may also pertain to other receptors.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional consequences of the catch step discussed in the manuscript.

claim: In several receptors kon to C is slower than diffusion and correlated with agonist potency.
source: As in AChRs, in several receptors kon to C is slower than diffusion and correlated with agonist potency (Dravid et al., 2008; Grewer, 1999; Lewis et al., 2003; Mortensen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to kinetic studies in other receptor systems.

claim: A catch-and-hold LFER is implied in other receptors (including a GPCR) because efficiency plots are linear.
source: Further, a catch-and-hold LFER is implied in other receptors (including a GPCR; Sykes et al., 2009) because efficiency plots are linear, with outliers that possibly indicate different η classes (Nayak et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on reanalysis of data from other receptor systems cited in previous work.

claim: In biological reactions, LFERs are empirical descriptors and more experiments are needed to determine the generality of η classes.
source: In biological reactions, LFERs are empirical descriptors and more experiments are needed to determine the generality of η classes.
evidence: This is a cautious statement acknowledging the need for further experimental validation.

claim: In AChRs, multiple η classes together preclude the appearance of a global affinity-efficacy correlation.
source: In AChRs, multiple η classes together preclude the appearance of a global affinity-efficacy correlation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the efficiency plots showing correlations only within individual classes.

claim: If η classes turn out to be common, then the consensus view that there is no correlation between affinity and efficacy needs to be reexamined.
source: If η classes turn out to be common, then the consensus view that there is no correlation between these agonist properties needs to be reexamined (Colquhoun, 1998; Kenakin and Onaran, 2002).
evidence: This is a speculation about the implications of the findings for receptor pharmacology.

claim: The clear correlation between log affinity and log efficacy within each class vanishes when agonists from different classes are lumped together.
source: The clear correlation between log affinity and log efficacy within each class vanishes when agonists from different classes are lumped together (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the efficiency plots in Figure 4B.

claim: Five η classes have been detected in AChRs but additional experiments could reveal more.
source: We detected 5 η classes in AChRs but additional experiments could reveal more.
evidence: This acknowledges the possibility of additional classes with further experimentation.

claim: Agonist classes with the highest and lowest η values have the greatest scatter and could be amalgams.
source: In particular, agonist classes with the highest and lowest η values have the greatest scatter and could be amalgams.
evidence: This is observed in the cluster analysis and efficiency plots.

claim: The ability to corral 76 different agonist-receptor combinations into just 5 classes represents a significant reduction in complexity.
source: Nonetheless, the ability to corral 76 different agonist-receptor combinations into just 5 classes represents a significant reduction in complexity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cluster analysis of all the data.

claim: η is a useful way to classify agonists and, possibly, binding sites.
source: If nothing else, η is a useful way to classify agonists and, possibly, binding sites.
evidence: This is a practical conclusion based on the ability of efficiency to group agonists and mutations.

claim: η could prove to be useful in CRC analysis because it allows EC50 to be computed from POmax and vice versa.
source: Also, η could prove to be useful CRC analysis because it allows EC50 to be computed from POmax and vice versa by using (Equation 3, Equation 4a, Equation 4b, Equation 4c, Equation 4d; Indurthi and Auerbach, 2021).
evidence: This is based on the mathematical relationships and is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Mutations of binding site residues segregate into the same 5 efficiency classes as do agonists.
source: Mutations of binding site residues segregate into the same 5 efficiency classes as do agonists.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the cluster analysis of mutation data in Figure 7.

claim: The observation that mutations segregate into the same efficiency classes as agonists supports the idea that an agonist at a binding site is much like an ordinary side chain, with exceptions.
source: This supports the idea that an agonist at a binding site is much like an ordinary side chain, with exceptions.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity in efficiency class distributions between agonists and mutations.

claim: Agonists are not linked covalently and so are both hypermobile in the pocket and free to come and go to serve as a signal.
source: Most importantly, agonists are not linked covalently and so are both hypermobile in the pocket and free to come and go to serve as a signal.
evidence: This is a fundamental difference between agonists and side chains based on chemical structure.

claim: By definition a bound agonist is more stable in O versus C but this is the opposite of most AChR wt side chains.
source: Also, by definition a bound agonist is more stable in O versus C (Figure 1A) but this is the opposite of most AChR wt side chains (Purohit et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on Φ-value analysis cited from previous work.

claim: η measurements reinforce the standard view that ligands only perturb the intrinsic activity of allosteric proteins.
source: η measurements reinforce the standard view that ligands only perturb the intrinsic activity of allosteric proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the efficiency measurements and the allosteric model.

claim: The pair of structural changes at the binding sites associated with energy changes in hold (ΔGHA-ΔGLA) and in catch (ΔGLA) are not known with certainty in AChRs.
source: In AChRs, the pair of structural changes at the binding sites associated with energy changes in hold (ΔGHA-ΔGLA) and in catch (ΔGLA) are not known with certainty.
evidence: This acknowledges the limitation that the structural basis of the energy changes is not fully determined.

claim: There are structures of apo-C and desensitized (perhaps the same as AOHA) states.
source: Although there are structures of apo-C (Zarkadas et al., 2022) and desensitized (perhaps the same as AOHA) (Auerbach, 2020; Rahman et al., 2020; Zarkadas et al., 2022), those of the three relevant liganded-closed intermediate states AC, ACLA and ACHA are not available.
evidence: This is based on citations to structural studies.

claim: The structures of the three relevant liganded-closed intermediate states AC, ACLA and ACHA are not available.
source: Although there are structures of apo-C (Zarkadas et al., 2022) and desensitized (perhaps the same as AOHA) (Auerbach, 2020; Rahman et al., 2020; Zarkadas et al., 2022), those of the three relevant liganded-closed intermediate states AC, ACLA and ACHA are not available.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in available structural data.

claim: If every agonist had a unique η then little could be said about the underlying conformational changes.
source: If every agonist had a unique η then little could be said about the underlying conformational changes.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the implications of the efficiency class observation.

claim: The existence of an η class and an LFER between catch-and-hold energy changes suggests that the corresponding structural changes are also correlated, although perhaps not linearly.
source: However, the existence of an η class and, therefore, an LFER between catch-and-hold energy changes suggests that the corresponding structural changes, too, are correlated, although perhaps not linearly.
evidence: This is inferred from the energy-structure relationship and the LFER observation.

claim: Catch and hold are two related stages of a single induced fit rearrangement of the binding site.
source: That is, catch and hold are two related stages of a single induced fit rearrangement of the binding site.
evidence: This is inferred from the LFER relationship between the two stages.

claim: At HA sites loop C covers ('caps') the aromatic pocket that appears to be contracted.
source: Regarding hold, at HA sites loop C covers ('caps') the aromatic pocket (Nys et al., 2013) that appears to be contracted.
evidence: This is based on structural studies cited in the text.

claim: Simulations suggest the possibilities that in the hold step the ligand flips its orientation.
source: Also, simulations suggest the possibilities that in the hold step the ligand flips its orientation (Tripathy et al., 2019), and that water is extruded from the binding interface (Young et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on computational studies cited in the text.

claim: Simulations suggest that water is extruded from the binding interface during hold.
source: Also, simulations suggest the possibilities that in the hold step the ligand flips its orientation (Tripathy et al., 2019), and that water is extruded from the binding interface (Young et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on computational studies cited in the text.

claim: Little is known about the catch rearrangement directly because the structures of neither end state have been solved.
source: Regarding catch, little is known about this rearrangement directly because the structures of neither end state have been solved.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in structural knowledge.

claim: Apo-C and AC are different states.
source: (Note that apo-C and AC are different).
evidence: This is a clarification about the distinction between unliganded and encounter complex states.

claim: Because of the LFER, all or some of the putative rearrangements in hold (cap, contract, flip, de-wet) also happen in catch, but perhaps to lesser extents.
source: However, because of the LFER, we hypothesize that all or some of the above putative rearrangements in hold (cap, contract, flip, de-wet) also happen in catch, but perhaps to lesser extents.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the LFER relationship between catch and hold.

claim: kon to C is slower than diffusion and correlated strongly with agonist potency.
source: Whereas kon to C is slower than diffusion and correlated strongly with agonist potency, kon to O is approximately at the diffusion limit and weakly agonist dependent.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements of association rate constants.

claim: kon to O is approximately at the diffusion limit and weakly agonist dependent.
source: Whereas kon to C is slower than diffusion and correlated strongly with agonist potency, kon to O is approximately at the diffusion limit and weakly agonist dependent.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements of association rate constants.

claim: Slow association to C cannot be attributed to the ligand itself but rather suggests that the hold stage of the induced fit removes a barrier(s) that otherwise prevents free entry of the ligand into the aromatic binding pocket.
source: Hence, slow association to C cannot be attributed to the ligand itself but rather suggests that the hold stage of the induced fit removes a barrier(s) that otherwise prevents free entry of the ligand into the aromatic binding pocket (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of association rate constants to C versus O.

claim: Neither the site of the encounter complex nor the nature of the barrier to ligand entry are known.
source: Neither the site of the encounter complex nor the nature of this barrier are known.
evidence: This acknowledges limitations in current knowledge.

claim: Loop C capping and pocket contraction would be expected to decrease rather than increase kon.
source: Because loop C capping and pocket contraction would be expected to decrease rather than increase kon, we speculate that in AChRs other, still-unidentified structural changes in hold serve to remove the barrier.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on structural considerations.

claim: In AChRs, other still-unidentified structural changes in hold serve to remove the barrier to ligand entry.
source: Because loop C capping and pocket contraction would be expected to decrease rather than increase kon, we speculate that in AChRs other, still-unidentified structural changes in hold serve to remove the barrier.
evidence: This is speculation based on the kinetic observations.

claim: Removing loop C eliminates activation by agonists but not unliganded gating.
source: Removing loop C eliminates activation by agonists but not unliganded gating (Purohit and Auerbach, 2009).
evidence: This is based on experimental results cited from previous work.

claim: Clamshell closure is necessary for transducing ligand binding energy into the receptor isomerization, but not for the global isomerization itself.
source: Apparently, clamshell closure is necessary for transducing ligand binding energy into the receptor isomerization, but not for the global isomerization itself.
evidence: This is inferred from the loop C deletion experiments.

claim: It is uncertain if other rearrangements in the binding site induced fit occur in unliganded gating after loop C removal.
source: However, it is uncertain if other rearrangements in the binding site induced fit occur in unliganded gating after loop C removal (see below).
evidence: This acknowledges uncertainty about the structural changes in unliganded gating.

claim: Energy change reflects a change in structure.
source: Energy change reflects a change in structure, so multiple η classes (logKdC/logKdO ratios) imply there are multiple pairs of C versus O (post-catch and post-hold) binding site conformations.
evidence: This is a fundamental principle relating energy and structure.

claim: Multiple η classes imply there are multiple pairs of C versus O (post-catch and post-hold) binding site conformations.
source: Energy change reflects a change in structure, so multiple η classes (logKdC/logKdO ratios) imply there are multiple pairs of C versus O (post-catch and post-hold) binding site conformations.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of five discrete efficiency classes.

claim: The existence of 5 discrete ΔGLA/ΔGHA ratios indicates that there are at least this many ACLA/ACHA binding site structural pairs.
source: The existence of 5 discrete ΔGLA/ΔGHA ratios indicates that there are at least this many ACLA/ACHA binding site structural pairs.
evidence: This is inferred from the energy-structure relationship and the observation of five efficiency classes.

claim: Possible combinations that give rise to 5 η classes are (number of ACLA/number of AOHA) 1/5, 2/3, 3/2, 4/2, and 5/1.
source: Possible combinations that give rise to 5 η classes are (number of ACLA/number of AOHA) 1/5, 2/3, 3/2, 4/2, and 5/1.
evidence: This is speculation about the structural basis of the efficiency classes.

claim: The discrete distribution of η classes suggests that the structural changes in the two stages of the induced fit also are discrete rather than continuous.
source: The discrete distribution of η classes suggests that the structural changes in the two stages of the induced fit also are discrete rather than continuous.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of discrete rather than continuous efficiency values.

claim: The AChR allosteric transition combines elements of induced fit (use of binding energy to drive a local rearrangement) and conformational selection (constitutive activity and the adoption of pre-existing target structures).
source: The AChR allosteric transition combines elements of induced fit (use of binding energy to drive a local rearrangement) and conformational selection (constitutive activity and the adoption of pre-existing target structures) (Changeux and Edelstein, 2005).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the efficiency measurements and is supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: The binding energy increase (in hold) occurs at the onset of the channel-opening gating isomerization.
source: The binding energy increase (in hold) occurs at the onset of the channel-opening gating isomerization (Grosman et al., 2000).
evidence: This is based on Φ-value analysis cited from previous work.

claim: The end states in the simple activation scheme do not represent single stable structures but rather ensembles made up of receptors having at least five distinct binding site structural pairs.
source: The existence of multiple, distinct C versus O structural pairs at each binding site indicates that the end states in the simple activation scheme (Figure 1B) do not represent single stable structures but rather ensembles made up of receptors having at least five distinct binding site structural pairs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of five efficiency classes.

claim: There could be five isomerization pathways that might culminate in five different structural perturbations of the gate region.
source: This raises the possibility that there could be five isomerization pathways that might culminate in five different structural perturbations of the gate region.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of five efficiency classes.

claim: There is no evidence in AChRs of any agonist-dependent variations in output properties (conductance or ion selectivity).
source: Although there is no evidence in AChRs of any agonist-dependent variations in output properties (conductance or ion selectivity), in other receptors functional output is agonist dependent (Kenakin and Christopoulos, 2013).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations in AChRs.

claim: In other receptors functional output is agonist dependent.
source: Although there is no evidence in AChRs of any agonist-dependent variations in output properties (conductance or ion selectivity), in other receptors functional output is agonist dependent (Kenakin and Christopoulos, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Efficiency measurements of receptors with biased agonism would test the possibility that η classes are associated with the phenomenon of biased agonism.
source: Efficiency measurements of these receptors would test the possibility that η classes are associated with the phenomenon of biased agonism (Ehlert, 2018).
evidence: This is a proposal for future experiments.

claim: There is a trend for agonists with cationic centers that occupy smaller volumes in vacuo to have greater η.
source: Finally, regarding the agonist (Figure 5), there is a trend for those with cationic centers that occupy smaller volumes in vacuo to have greater η (Indurthi and Auerbach, 2021).
evidence: This is an observation based on analysis of agonist structures and efficiencies, supported by citation.

claim: Agonists with larger volumes tend to use a greater fraction of their binding energy for catch.
source: That is, agonists with larger volumes tend to use a greater fraction of their binding energy for catch.
evidence: This is inferred from the trend relating agonist size to efficiency.

claim: The volume of the binding pocket appears to be smaller in O versus C in AChRs and other receptors.
source: In AChRs and other receptors, the volume of the binding pocket appears to be smaller in O versus C (Tripathy et al., 2019), so it is also possible that unfavorable VdW interactions caused by pocket contraction guide the selection of (for example) the target O structure, to decrease η.
evidence: This is based on computational studies cited in the text.

claim: Unfavorable VdW interactions caused by pocket contraction may guide the selection of the target O structure, to decrease η.
source: In AChRs and other receptors, the volume of the binding pocket appears to be smaller in O versus C (Tripathy et al., 2019), so it is also possible that unfavorable VdW interactions caused by pocket contraction guide the selection of (for example) the target O structure, to decrease η.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism relating agonist size to efficiency.

claim: The relationship between catch and hold energy change and the corresponding structural elements (agonist, protein, water) is complex and further investigations are needed.
source: The relationship between catch and hold energy change and the corresponding structural elements (agonist, protein, water) is complex and further investigations are needed.
evidence: This acknowledges the complexity and need for further research.

claim: The catch-and-hold LFER implied by an η class indicates that structure (energy) changes in these two binding site rearrangements are related.
source: The catch-and-hold LFER implied by an η class indicates that structure (energy) changes in these two binding site rearrangements are related.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of efficiency classes.

claim: Microscopic reversibility demands that if catch promotes hold, then hold promotes catch.
source: Microscopic reversibility demands that if catch promotes hold, then hold promotes catch.
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of thermodynamics.

claim: The bidirectional linkage between catch and hold is the tip of an iceberg, and the entire AChR activation cascade is linked as an extended, multi-stage LFER.
source: Below, we present evidence suggesting that this bidirectional linkage is the tip of an iceberg, and that the entire AChR activation cascade - from an agonist at the encounter complex to water at the gate (AC to AO) - is linked as an extended, multi-stage LFER (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on multiple lines of evidence discussed in the manuscript.

claim: There have been several proposals in AChRs regarding structural changes that link the neurotransmitter sites and the gate, but these are difficult to assess because they are without corroborating energy measurements.
source: There have been several proposals in AChRs regarding structural changes that link the neurotransmitter sites and the gate, but these are difficult to assess because they are without corroborating energy measurements.
evidence: This acknowledges limitations in previous structural studies.

claim: η measurements reveal a binding-gating energy link at the agonist site, but lack corroborating structural information.
source: Likewise, η measurements reveal a binding-gating energy link at the agonist site, but lack corroborating structural information.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the current study.

claim: Separate activation domains in AChR activation have been identified.
source: However, separate activation domains in AChR activation have been identified.
evidence: This is based on previous experimental work on AChR activation.

claim: η calibrates the catch-hold connection at the agonist binding site.
source: For instance, η calibrates the catch-hold connection at the agonist binding site, mutations decouple the ECD-TMD interface (Cymes and Grosman, 2021; Shi et al., 2023) and interactions between gate residues and pore water have been investigated (Beckstein and Sansom, 2006; Rasaiah et al., 2008; Yazdani et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a conclusion of the current study.

claim: Mutations decouple the ECD-TMD interface.
source: For instance, η calibrates the catch-hold connection at the agonist binding site, mutations decouple the ECD-TMD interface (Cymes and Grosman, 2021; Shi et al., 2023) and interactions between gate residues and pore water have been investigated (Beckstein and Sansom, 2006; Rasaiah et al., 2008; Yazdani et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on cited experimental work.

claim: Interactions between gate residues and pore water have been investigated.
source: For instance, η calibrates the catch-hold connection at the agonist binding site, mutations decouple the ECD-TMD interface (Cymes and Grosman, 2021; Shi et al., 2023) and interactions between gate residues and pore water have been investigated (Beckstein and Sansom, 2006; Rasaiah et al., 2008; Yazdani et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on cited computational and experimental work.

claim: Analyses of the gating transition state suggest that there are 5 discrete domain rearrangements.
source: Analyses of the gating transition state suggest that there are 5 discrete domain rearrangements (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on Φ-value analysis discussed in the manuscript.

claim: In opening, hold is followed by movements of the ECD, TMD, gate region, and, finally, pore water and membrane lipids.
source: In opening, hold is followed by movements of the ECD, TMD, gate region, and, finally, pore water and membrane lipids (Gupta et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on Φ-value analysis cited from previous work.

claim: When an unliganded AChR opens constitutively, kon increases to approach the diffusion limit, and also loses its agonist dependence.
source: As mentioned above, when an unliganded AChR opens constitutively, kon increases to approach the diffusion limit, and also loses its agonist dependence.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements of association rate constants.

claim: With loop C intact, adopting the global O shape in the absence of agonists is sufficient to induce the local change in structure that removes the entry barrier, in hold.
source: This indicates that with loop C intact, adopting the global O shape in the absence of agonists is sufficient to induce the local change in structure that removes the entry barrier, in hold.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that kon increases in the O state.

claim: A distant mutation (for example, of a gate residue) increases constitutive opening and also influences the ligand association rate constant, which is evidence that binding and gating are entangled.
source: That a distant mutation (for example, of a gate residue) increases constitutive opening and also influences the ligand association rate constant is evidence that binding and gating are entangled.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations showing long-range coupling.

claim: Everything in the protein's activation cascade, AC to AO, is energy-linked in a reversible, extended LFER.
source: This result, along with η and Φ measurements, leads us to propose that everything in the protein's activation cascade, AC to AO, is energy-linked in a reversible, extended LFER.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on multiple lines of evidence including efficiency, Φ-values, and association rate constants.

claim: In the extended LFER sequence, each individual domain energy change (rearrangement) influences those of its neighbors, bidirectionally.
source: In this sequence, each individual domain energy change (rearrangement) influences those of its neighbors, bidirectionally.
evidence: This is part of the extended LFER hypothesis.

claim: Usually, the first link in activation (after the encounter complex) is catch-and-hold, and the last is gate-and-water.
source: Usually, the first link in activation (after the encounter complex) is catch-and-hold, and the last is gate-and-water.
evidence: This describes the typical sequence of events in agonist-induced activation.

claim: In a LFER the consequence of a perturbation propagates both forward and backward.
source: However, in a LFER the consequence of a perturbation propagates both forward and backward, so a gate mutation would also perturb the agonist site and one at the ECD-TMD would induce rearrangements both there and at the gate.
evidence: This is a property of LFERs and is supported by experimental observations.

claim: An extended LFER offers a way to transfer energy (change structure) over distance by using only local domain rearrangements.
source: An extended LFER offers a way to transfer energy (change structure) over distance by using only local domain rearrangements.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism for long-range coupling in allosteric proteins.

claim: In AChRs, the allosteric transition appears to be a energy-coupled chain of domain rearrangements that crosses seamlessly the traditional divide between binding and gating.
source: In AChRs, the allosteric transition appears to be a energy-coupled chain of domain rearrangements that crosses seamlessly the traditional divide between binding and gating.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the extended LFER hypothesis and supporting evidence.

claim: η is at the core of receptor operation insofar as it links the induced fit with the conformational gating cascade.
source: η is at the core receptor operation insofar as it links the induced fit with the conformational gating cascade, Φ reveals the cascade's components (and the sequence of domain rearrangements), and kon to O reveals that a reverse cascade, gate→binding site, exists without agonists.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the central role of efficiency in receptor function.

claim: Φ reveals the cascade's components and the sequence of domain rearrangements.
source: η is at the core receptor operation insofar as it links the induced fit with the conformational gating cascade, Φ reveals the cascade's components (and the sequence of domain rearrangements), and kon to O reveals that a reverse cascade, gate→binding site, exists without agonists.
evidence: This is based on Φ-value analysis from previous work.

claim: kon to O reveals that a reverse cascade, gate→binding site, exists without agonists.
source: η is at the core receptor operation insofar as it links the induced fit with the conformational gating cascade, Φ reveals the cascade's components (and the sequence of domain rearrangements), and kon to O reveals that a reverse cascade, gate→binding site, exists without agonists.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that kon increases in the O state.

claim: Transit across the whole extended LFER is rapid (~5 μs).
source: Transit across the whole extended LFER is rapid (~5 μs; Lape et al., 2008), with each interemdiate states lasting on the order of 100 ns (Gupta et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on kinetic measurements cited from previous work.

claim: Each intermediate state in the extended LFER lasts on the order of 100 ns.
source: Transit across the whole extended LFER is rapid (~5 μs; Lape et al., 2008), with each interemdiate states lasting on the order of 100 ns (Gupta et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on kinetic analysis cited from previous work.

claim: HEK cells obtained from ATCC (CRL-1573, lot no. 57925149) are authenticated using STR profiling and tested free of mycoplasma contamination.
source: HEK cells obtained from ATCC (CRL-1573, lot no. 57925149) are authenticated using STR profiling and tested free of mycoplasma contamination.
evidence: This is a statement about the quality control of cell lines used in the experiments.

claim: L0 is 7.4x10–7 at Vm=-100 mV and reduced e-fold by a 60 mV depolarization.
source: L0 is 7.4x10–7 at Vm=-100 mV and reduced e-fold by a 60 mV depolarization (Nayak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an experimental measurement cited from previous work.

claim: L0 is 5.2x10–7 at Vm=-70 mV as well as in experiments at Vm = +70 mV plus εS450W.
source: Hence, we calculate that L0 is 5.2x10–7 at Vm=-70 mV as well as in our experiments at Vm = +70 mV plus εS450W.
evidence: This is calculated from the voltage dependence of L0 and the effect of the background mutation.

claim: The background mutations εL269F and εE181W increase L0 by 179- and 5.5-fold respectively (1084-fold for the pair) without affecting KdC.
source: These were εL269F (located in the M2 helix) and εE181W (located in strand β9) that increase the L0 by 179- and 5.5-fold (1084-fold for the pair) without effecting KdC.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements of the effects of these mutations.
